Name: Maker's Mark Bourbon Whisky
Details: If you're looking for a smooth, sweet and easy-to-drink whisky, you've found it. Still made to his unique recipe, this full-flavored bourbon is subtly woody with flavors of vanilla, caramel and fruit. It's easy to drink neat, and can pull its weight in a cocktail. Name: Jägermeister Liqueur

The herbs and spices are blended together then steeped in water and alcohol to extract flavors before resting in oak barrels for nearly a year. The base is then mixed with water, caramelized sugar and alcohol before being bottled. Before this herbal liqueur reaches your glass, Jägermeister undergoes 383 quality checks from start to finish. Jägermeister’s flavor consists of five distinct notes, sweet, bitter, citrus, spicy, and aromatic, working together to create a balanced cordial that is unlike anything else. Initial tasting notes of anise, fennel, coffee, orange, burnt sugar and cola come to the forefront with a smooth, complex finish that is not overly sweet. Originally a celebratory drink for hunters, it's the ideal drink to mark any special occasion. Celebrate big wins, birthdays and milestone moments or kick off a well-deserved weekend with this iconic liqueur. The best way to enjoy Jägermeister is in the form of an ice-cold shot, served straight from the freezer. Jägermeister also brings complex flavor to a variety of classic cocktails. Embrace originality and try a Jägermeister Mule, Jägermeister Old Fashioned or Jägermeister and Tonic for delicious mixed drinks. Jägermeister has 35% ABV and should be enjoyed responsibly. Jägermeister is embraced by those who push the boundaries and rewrite the rules in every field. Long may it continue…

Sakura leaves and flowers are handpicked in spring, with Sencha and Gyokuro teas being plucked in summer. Family tradition states that "V.O." stands for "Very Own," as this was a whisky blend created for Joseph E. Seagram's own family. Others claim that the initials stand for "Very Old" in keeping with the distillers assertion that is was a blend of very old Canadian Whiskies. The story tells how Joseph's son, Thomas, had the distillery's blender, William Hortop, prepare a whisky blend for his personal use to celebrate his upcoming marriage in 1913 to Dorothy Pearson. Upon tasting the special blend, Joseph insisted that the family blend be put on the market. It went on to become one of Seagram's biggest sellers.
